issues.issue: The covenant is conditioned on "the enactment of concurrent legislation ... having the same effect as this Part," yet the federal enacting statute in Part II (Section 15.1 Reservations) attaches conditions that vary the compact's terms. A court could be asked whether legislation containing such reservations is legislation "having the same effect," and what the covenant binds the parties to.

Section 1.1 names "this Act" the Delaware River Basin Compact, while Section 1.2(c) defines "Compact" as Part I of the act only. The two provisions give the same word different reach, so it is unclear whether Part II (the reservations and state effectuation sections) is part of the Compact.

"Area of drainage into the Delaware River and its tributaries" fixes no boundary for ground water or for land whose surface drainage is diverted, so the geographic reach of "Basin" is indeterminate. Because Section 2.7 limits the commission's powers to "the limits of the basin," the vagueness is jurisdictional.

Defining "Compact" as Part I only leaves the Part II federal reservations (Section 15.1) outside the defined term, although they expressly override compact sections such as 2.2, 3.7 and 11.5. A court could be asked whether provisions saying "nothing contained in the Compact" reach those reservations at all.

"Net induced adverse effects, whether or not compensated for" is a cost component with no method or boundary of measurement stated. The term drives assessments under Section 4.3 and cost allocations under Section 11.4, so its indeterminacy is operative.

"Facility" is defined by an open catch-all — "any and all things and appurtenances necessary, useful or convenient" — appended to a list of water-related structures, raising an ejusdem generis question about how far beyond water works it reaches. Whether privately owned industrial works such as well pads are "facilities" acquired or operated "for the beneficial use of water resources" is genuinely contestable.

"Any appropriate branch, department, bureau or division thereof, as the case may be" supplies no criterion of appropriateness, so which federal entity is bound as the "Federal government" in a given section is left open.

"Project" — "any work, service or activity which is separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission, or any separate facility undertaken ... for the conservation, utilization, control, development or management of water resources" — is syntactically ambiguous as to whether "by the commission" qualifies the whole clause and whether privately undertaken industrial activity such as a gas well falls within it. The qualifying phrases "which can be established and utilized independently" and "considered as a separate entity for purposes of evaluation" give no workable boundary.

Read with Section 3.8, which subjects projects "undertaken by any person, corporation or governmental authority" to commission approval, the definition's reference to planning, financing or identification "by the commission" cannot easily be squared with the referral-and-review regime. A court must decide whether 3.8 reaches activities the commission never planned, financed or identified.

"Water resources" is defined to "include" water and "related natural resources in, on, under, or above the ground, including related uses of land" — an inclusive, unbounded formula with no test of relatedness. Whether subsurface minerals such as natural gas, or the land uses that extract them, are "related natural resources" is the contestable point.

This is a legislative finding, not an operative grant, yet it declares the management of basin water resources to be "public purposes" in terms broad enough to be argued as expanding the commission's operative powers under Article 3. A court could be asked whether the finding controls or merely explains the operative sections.

The declaration that the compact provides for "a joint exercise of such powers of sovereignty" is a finding that parties invoke against the operative reservations of state authority in Sections 5.5, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c). Whether the finding qualifies those savings clauses is a question of construction.

The finding that "a single administrative agency is therefore essential" sits against Section 1.5, which directs preservation and use of existing offices and agencies, and against the savings clauses in Sections 5.5, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c). Which prevails when the commission and a state agency both claim a subject is left open.

The finding that the basin's waters "are ample to meet all presently projected demands" cannot be squared with Sections 10.2 and 10.4, which presuppose water shortages, protected areas and supply emergencies. A party could argue the finding limits the shortage powers, or that the finding is spent.

The declared purpose "to make secure and protect present developments within the states" pulls against the operative approval requirement in Section 3.8 and the withdrawal controls in Article 10, which can defeat existing developments. Which reading of the compact's purpose governs interpretation of those operative powers is contestable.

Section 1.4's saving of congressional powers is qualified in Part II by Section 15.1(b) and 15.1(s), which are themselves expressed as "applicable to the extent not inconsistent with Section 1.4." The circular cross-reference leaves it unclear which text yields when they conflict.

Section 1.5's direction to preserve existing agencies "to the extent not inconsistent with the compact" cannot be squared straightforwardly with Section 1.3(c)'s declaration that a single administrative agency is essential. The phrase "to the fullest extent it finds feasible and advantageous" also leaves the duty entirely to the commission's own judgment.

The renewal condition — continuation "if not later than 20 years nor sooner than 25 years prior to the termination" none of the signatory states gives notice — combines an inverted time window with a double negative, and is readily read two ways. It also speaks only of "signatory states," leaving the federal signatory's power to terminate unaddressed.

Paragraph (b) speaks of termination "by operation of paragraph (a)," but paragraph (a) operates to continue the compact; termination results from state notice, not from the paragraph. The winding-up is also left "in such manner as may be provided by act of the Congress," with no fallback if Congress does not act.

Calling the commission "an agency and instrumentality of the governments of the respective signatory parties" cannot be squared with Section 15.1(m), which provides that for the enumerated federal statutes the commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency." The commission's status for immunity and procedural purposes therefore turns on which provision governs.

Section 2.2 provides that the federal commissioner serves "during the term of office of the President," while Section 15.1(d) provides that he "shall serve at the pleasure of the President." The two cannot both be given effect on tenure, as the compact's own endnote acknowledges.

The rule that an alternate "shall serve during the term of the member appointing him, subject to removal at the pleasure of the member" conflicts with Section 15.1(d), which makes the federal alternate serve at the pleasure of the President rather than of the member. The saving phrase "unless otherwise provided by law of the signatory party" may or may not absorb that.

Section 2.4 says members and alternates "shall serve without compensation," while Section 15.1(r) provides that, "the provisions of Sections 2.4 and 2.6 ... notwithstanding," the federal member and alternate may be paid by the United States. The two provisions state opposite rules for the same officers.

"A majority of the membership" does not say whether it means a majority of the full membership or of those present and voting, and Section 14.5(a) uses the contrasting phrase "majority of the full membership." The difference decides whether business can be done with absent members.

Section 2.6 leaves the appointment of an advisor to "each member in his discretion," but New York's § 632(1) mandates that its member's advisor "shall be the mayor of the city of New York or his designee." The state enactment and the compact provision cannot both be given full effect.

The commission may act outside the basin "whenever such action may be necessary or convenient to effectuate its powers or duties within the basin," a standard with no articulated limit and set entirely by the commission's own discretion. "Convenient" in particular carries no measurable boundary.

Section 3.2(b) requires a water resources program covering "such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine," while Section 13.1's counterpart, Section 13.2, fixes "the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period." Because 3.2 is expressly to be exercised "in accordance with Article 13," the two statements of the program's period must be reconciled.

The grant to allocate waters "in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment" is hard to square with Section 3.3(b), which says no such action "shall be deemed to constitute an apportionment of the waters of the basin among the parties." What the commission is doing when it allocates, and with what legal effect, comes out only when the two are read together.

The paragraph uses two different unanimity requirements — "unanimous consent of the parties to the ... decree" and "unanimous consent of its members" — in successive clauses governing overlapping subject matter. Which consent is required for a given emergency action, and for how long "such limited time" runs, is left uncertain.

Paragraph (b)'s statement that no allocation constitutes an apportionment cannot be squared with the opening of Section 3.3, which directs the commission to allocate "in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment." A court would have to decide whether allocations create enforceable entitlements at all.

"Any proper party deeming itself aggrieved" is undefined, and the section gives no test of who qualifies for de novo Supreme Court review as against ordinary judicial review "in any court of competent jurisdiction." The line between an "out-of-basin diversion" action and "any other action of the commission" is equally unmarked.

The waiver is followed by an exception permitting proceedings "to increase diversions or compensating releases in connection with such increased diversions" but not decreases, though the waiver itself covers both. Whether that asymmetry is deliberate or a drafting slip governs what modifications remain available.

Section 3.5's flat prohibitions on impeding the decree sit against Section 3.3(a), which lets the commission by unanimous vote increase or decrease decree diversions and releases in an emergency. The opening "except as specifically provided in Sections 3.3 and 3.4" is the only bridge, and its scope is contestable.

Paragraph (h) is a general catch-all — "such other and different powers ... and ... all powers necessary or convenient to carry out its express powers or which may be reasonably implied therefrom" — appended to seven enumerated specifics. Whether it expands the commission's authority beyond the enumeration or is confined by it is a classic ejusdem generis dispute.

Section 3.7's grant of rate-setting power "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party" is directly cut back by Section 15.1(b), which forbids charges for withdrawals lawfully free at the effective date and for commercial navigation. The two cannot both be given full effect as written.

"No project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin" turns approval jurisdiction on an undefined threshold — "substantial effect" — with no measure supplied here or in Article 13. The same is true of the approval test, "substantially impair or conflict with the comprehensive plan."

Section 3.8 subjects projects undertaken "by any person, corporation or governmental authority" to review, but Section 1.2(g) defines "project" by reference to work "separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission." Whether private undertakings the commission never identified are within Section 3.8 is only resolvable by reading the two together.

The introductory clause reads "To this end, but with limitation thereto, the commission may," where the parallel provisions (Sections 3.5, 4.1 and 3.6(b)) read "without limitation thereto." The apparent omission of "out" reverses the sense of the sentence, making the enumerated powers exhaustive rather than illustrative.

Section 4.1's grant of power to build and operate water supply works "without limitation thereto" runs up against Section 4.5's proviso that nothing authorizes the commission "to engage in the business of distributing water." Where supply ends and distribution begins is settled only by reading the two together.

The enumerated purposes for storage and release close with "and other purposes," a catch-all with no limiting principle after a list of water-quality and public-benefit purposes. Its reach against the specific enumeration is contestable.

The prohibition on permitting augmentation of flow to be diminished by diversion excepts diversions "duly authorized by this compact," which must be read against Sections 3.3(a) and 3.5, protecting decree diversions from commission interference. Whether decree diversions are within the exception or beyond the prohibition altogether is left unclear.

Assessments may be laid on water users "specially benefited thereby to a measurable extent," and "no such assessment shall exceed the actual benefit to any water user" — two benefit standards with no method of measurement stated. Whether "actual benefit" is measured as in Section 1.2(d)'s definition of cost is not said.

Section 4.4 requires a public hearing "on each proposed project" under Article 4, while Section 14.4(b) enumerates the occasions on which hearings are required and adds "all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing." Whether the ten-day notice regime of 14.4(b) governs each Article 4 project hearing must be worked out between them.

"The business of distributing water" is not defined, and the same sentence grants power to provide "transmission facilities," which may amount to distribution. The boundary between an authorized transmission facility and a forbidden distribution business is unmarked.

The pollution standard — that waste "shall not injuriously affect waters of the basin as contemplated by the comprehensive plan" — has no stated threshold and is anchored to a plan the commission itself writes under Section 13.1. "Injuriously affect" carries no measurable boundary.

The covenant to "enact any necessary legislation" and to keep waters "in a satisfactory condition" describes the required condition only by open-ended adjectives — "safe and satisfactory," "suitable," "free from unsightly or malodorous nuisances." What performance would discharge a signatory's covenant cannot be determined from the words.

Enforcement orders are made "reviewable in any court of competent jurisdiction," a phrase New York's § 634 redefines for its courts and Section 15.1(p) overlays with exclusive-sounding federal district court original jurisdiction. Where review of a cease order lies is resolved only by reading the three together.
